patient.name: Daniel Okafor
patient.setting: GP surgery (telephone triage, then a face-to-face review)
patient.complaint: Runny nose, sore throat and cough for 3 days, caught from his son
background: Secondary school PE teacher in Lewisham
His 3 year old son Tobi had a cold, then a barking cough at night

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with coryza, sore throat and no focal chest signs, or a young child with a barking cough and stridor (croup); also 'Which is the most likely causative organism?'.

points: Daniel, 34, has had a **runny nose** and **sneezing** for 3 days.
Scratchy **sore throat**, blocked nose and a dry cough.
It is **January**; half his class is off sick.

steps.lead: Daniel's nose and throat are infected, almost certainly by a **virus** such as rhinovirus.
Two risk factors: it is **winter**, and he is in close **contact** with an ill son and a classroom of teenagers.

points: Nasal mucosa swollen with clear discharge.
Chest: **clear**, no crackles, no bronchial breathing.

steps.lead: Daniel has the textbook picture: **coryza**, sore throat, cough, low-grade fever, an erythematous throat and **no focal chest findings**.

steps.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis for Daniel?
steps.r: Coryza, sore throat and cough with a **clear chest** and low fever is a **viral URTI**. No exudate, so not bacterial tonsillitis; no chest signs, so not pneumonia.

points: His son **Tobi, 3**, started with a cold last week.
Then a **barking, seal-like cough**, worse at night.

steps.lead: Tobi had **croup**: a URTI of the larynx and trachea, usually **parainfluenza**, in a child aged **6 months to 6 years**, causing **stridor**.

visual.title: Who gets croup?
visual.label: Tobi 3 years
visual.caption: Barking cough and stridor in this age band = croup until proven otherwise.

steps.title: Same viruses, different level of the airway
head: Feature
Common cold
Croup
Pneumonia (LRTI)

steps.lead: Daniel is safety-netted: **otitis media** or **sinusitis** can follow, and high fever, breathlessness or chest pain would mean it has spread to the chest.

steps.text: Stridor is **inspiratory** and comes from the upper airway (larynx). Wheeze is mainly **expiratory** and comes from the small airways.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate investigation?' where the answer is usually none (clinical diagnosis); in a severe case, bloods and a chest X-ray to exclude pneumonia.

steps.q: Daniel asks for a swab 'to see which bug it is'. What confirms the diagnosis?
steps.r: A URTI is a **clinical diagnosis**. Swabs and PCR do not change management in a well adult.

steps.lead: Daniel's history and a clear chest are enough: **no tests** are needed on day 3.

points: Day 6: fever now **39.2°C**, and he is **breathless** on the stairs.
Sharp pain on breathing in on the right.
Seen face to face the same day.

steps.lead: High fever, breathlessness and chest pain are emergency features, so Daniel now has **bloods and a chest X-ray** to exclude pneumonia.

steps.title: Daniel's bloods on day 6
steps.text: A mildly raised CRP with a normal white count fits a viral illness, not lobar pneumonia.

visual.title: Daniel's chest X-ray
visual.caption: Clear lung fields, no consolidation or effusion: no pneumonia. He has a viral URTI with a muscular chest pain from coughing.

steps.text: In URTI questions, a **clear chest on examination** is the clue that says no X-ray. Focal crackles or bronchial breathing push you to pneumonia and a CXR.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate management?' where the answer is self-care with paracetamol and ibuprofen and a review if not improving, not antibiotics; phenoxymethylpenicillin only if bacterial infection is suspected.

steps.lead: Daniel's plan is **self-care**: paracetamol, ibuprofen, fluids and rest, with a **xylometazoline** spray for his blocked nose and a review in **3-4 days** if not improving.

steps.q: Day 3, clear chest, well. Daniel asks for antibiotics. What do you do?
o: Self-care and review if not improving
steps.r: Most URTIs are **viral and self-limiting**; antibiotics do not help and cause side effects and resistance.

visual.title: Days since onset
visual.label: Daniel day 3
visual.caption: Review in 3-4 days if not improving, or sooner with red flags.

steps.text: Xylometazoline is for **short-term** use only (up to about 7 days): longer use causes **rebound congestion** (rhinitis medicamentosa).

steps.title: URTI management
nodes: Red flags (high fever, breathless, chest pain)? → assess for LRTI
Blocked nose → short course of xylometazoline
Review in 3-4 days if not improving
Bacterial infection suspected → phenoxymethylpenicillin (clarithromycin if allergic)
steps.caption: Antibiotics are the exception, not the rule.

steps.lead: Daniel's X-ray was clear, so no antibiotic. If a **bacterial** cause were suspected, it would be **phenoxymethylpenicillin**, or **clarithromycin** if penicillin allergic.

steps.text: Tobi's croup is treated with a single dose of oral **dexamethasone** (0.15 mg/kg), whatever the severity; severe stridor at rest needs hospital and nebulised adrenaline.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: the organism (rhinovirus for colds, parainfluenza for croup), why croup causes stridor in small children, or why otitis media follows a cold.

steps.lead: Daniel's runny, blocked nose is the mucosa's response: **inflammation, oedema and extra mucus**.
Tobi's **subglottic** airway is tiny, so a little swelling narrows it a lot: barking cough and **inspiratory stridor**.

steps.q: Why does the same virus give Tobi stridor but Daniel only a sore throat?
o: Children's narrow airway is disproportionately affected by swelling
steps.r: Airway resistance rises steeply as radius falls: **mucosal swelling in a narrow paediatric subglottis** causes obstruction.

steps.title: How a cold becomes otitis media
nodes: Bacteria ascend to the middle ear

steps.lead: If Daniel develops ear pain, damaged mucosa and poor clearance will have let bacteria up the **Eustachian tube** (otitis media) or into his **sinuses**.

visual.title: Daniel's recovery
visual.caption: Peaks around day 3 and settles within about a week as his immune response clears the virus.

steps.lead: Daniel gets better in about **a week** without antibiotics: his **immune response** clears the virus and there is no ongoing tissue damage.

mcq.q: Which virus most commonly causes the common cold?
What age group is typically affected by croup?

o: Harsh inspiratory sound from laryngeal obstruction
mcq.r: **Stridor** is a harsh inspiratory sound from upper airway (laryngeal) obstruction.

mcq.q: Which is a common complication of URTI from secondary bacterial infection?
What is the gold standard for diagnosing a URTI?
In a severe case, which tests are done to exclude pneumonia?
What is first-line management of an uncomplicated URTI?
mcq.r: **Self-care**, review in 3-4 days if not improving.

mcq.q: Which antibiotic is used if a bacterial URTI is suspected in a penicillin-allergic patient?
Why do most URTIs resolve on their own?
o: Host immune response clears the virus
mcq.r: Self-limiting in about **a week**, driven by the host immune response.

technique.stem: A 27 year old woman has a 2 day history of runny nose, sneezing, sore throat and a dry cough. It is December and her partner has similar symptoms. Her temperature is 37.6°C and pulse rate 82 bpm. Her throat is red without exudate. Her chest is clear on auscultation.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis: where in the airway is the problem?
Coryza, winter, contact, no exudate, **no chest signs**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Bronchitis: a productive cough dominates, often with wheeze.
Allergic rhinitis has no fever or sore throat, and is seasonal.
No tonsillar exudate and a cough lowers Centor.
Pneumonia gives focal chest signs and higher fever.

steps.x: **D. Common cold.** Coryza + clear chest = upper airway virus.

technique.stem: A 40 year old man has a 3 day history of nasal congestion, sore throat and cough. He is eating and drinking normally. His temperature is 37.7°C, pulse rate 80 bpm, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air. His chest is clear.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?

steps.x: Investigation: would any test change management?

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: CXR is for severe cases to exclude pneumonia.
Bloods are for severe cases.
He has a dry cough; sputum culture does not help.
Swabs do not change management of a cold.

steps.x: **C. No investigation.** URTI is a clinical diagnosis.

technique.stem: A 31 year old woman has a 2 day history of a blocked nose, runny nose, sore throat and mild cough. She feels tired but is otherwise well. Her temperature is 37.5°C, pulse rate 78 bpm and BP 118/70 mmHg. Her chest is clear. She asks for something to help.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate management?

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Self-care**: paracetamol, ibuprofen, and review in 3-4 days if not improving.

elim: Antibiotics do not help a viral URTI.
Clarithromycin is for suspected bacterial infection with allergy.
Steroids have no role in a cold.
Penicillin V only if bacterial infection is suspected.

technique.stem: A 2 year old boy has had a cold for 2 days. Tonight he has a barking cough, a hoarse voice and a harsh noise on breathing in. His temperature is 37.9°C. He is alert and pink.
technique.q: Which is the most likely cause of the noise on breathing in?
o: Foreign body in the right main bronchus

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Small airway narrowing gives expiratory wheeze.
Epiglottitis: toxic, drooling, high fever, no barking cough.
A bronchial foreign body gives unilateral wheeze, sudden onset.
Pleural inflammation gives pleuritic pain and a rub.

steps.x: **E. Subglottic narrowing.** Croup stridor = swollen narrow paediatric subglottis.

practice.stem: A 45 year old man has a 4 day history of a runny nose, sneezing, sore throat and a dry cough. His wife and daughter have had similar symptoms. His temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 84 bpm, BP 128/80 mmHg and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. His throat is red without exudate. There are no added sounds on chest auscultation.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Coryza, sore throat, cough, low-grade fever and a clear chest in a household cluster is a viral URTI. Pneumonia would give focal chest signs.

clues: runny nose, sneezing, sore throat and a dry cough
no added sounds on chest auscultation
steps.x: Upper airway symptoms, contacts, **no focal chest findings**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Sinusitis needs facial pain and purulent discharge, often beyond 10 days.
No exudate and a cough present.
Pneumonia gives crackles or bronchial breathing.
Glandular fever: exudate, posterior nodes, splenomegaly.

practice.stem: A 2 year old girl has had a runny nose for 2 days. During the night she developed a barking cough, a hoarse cry and a harsh noise when breathing in. Her temperature is 38.0°C, pulse rate 130 bpm, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. She is not drooling.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A coryzal prodrome, barking cough, hoarseness and inspiratory stridor in a 2 year old is croup (laryngotracheobronchitis). Epiglottitis gives drooling and a toxic child without a barking cough.

steps.x: Paediatric diagnosis with a noisy breath.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Epiglottitis: high fever, drooling, toxic, tripod position.
Bronchiolitis is in infants under 1 with wheeze and crackles.
A foreign body is sudden onset without a prodrome or fever.
Whooping cough has paroxysms with an inspiratory whoop, no stridor at rest.

steps.x: **C. Croup.** Barking cough + stridor at 6 months to 6 years.

practice.stem: A 3 year old boy has a barking cough and inspiratory stridor at night after 2 days of coryza. His temperature is 37.9°C. A diagnosis of croup is made.
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
practice.e: Croup is caused by parainfluenza virus. Hib causes epiglottitis, RSV causes bronchiolitis and Bordetella causes whooping cough.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Bordetella causes whooping cough.
Hib causes epiglottitis.
RSV causes bronchiolitis in infants.
Rhinovirus causes the common cold.

practice.stem: A 24 year old woman has a 3 day history of a blocked, runny nose, sneezing and a mild sore throat. Her temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 76 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg. Her chest is clear. A viral upper respiratory tract infection is diagnosed.
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
practice.e: The common cold is most often rhinovirus. Adenovirus and influenza are also listed causes but are less common; EBV causes glandular fever.

steps.x: Commonest organism for a common cold.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Adenovirus causes URTI but is less common; often conjunctivitis too.
EBV gives glandular fever.
Influenza gives abrupt high fever and myalgia.
VZV causes chickenpox and shingles.

steps.x: **D. Rhinovirus.** Commonest cause of the common cold.

practice.stem: A 4 year old girl had a cold with runny nose and cough 5 days ago. Since last night she has been pulling at her right ear, crying and feverish. Her temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 128 bpm and BP 96/60 mmHg. The right tympanic membrane is red and bulging.
practice.q: Which is the most likely complication of her URTI?
practice.e: A red, bulging drum with fever and ear pain after a cold is acute otitis media, from bacteria ascending the Eustachian tube. Mastoiditis adds swelling behind the ear.

steps.x: A secondary bacterial complication of URTI.
After a cold, ear pain and a **bulging drum**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Cholesteatoma is chronic, with foul discharge and hearing loss.
Mastoiditis: tender swelling behind the ear, pinna pushed forward.
Otitis externa affects the canal, with pain on moving the pinna.
Glue ear is a dull retracted drum without acute pain or fever.

steps.x: **A. Acute otitis media.** Cold + bulging red drum.

practice.stem: A 38 year old man has had a runny nose, sore throat and dry cough for 3 days. His temperature is 37.7°C, pulse rate 82 bpm, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. A viral upper respiratory tract infection is suspected.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on chest examination?
o: Bronchial breathing at the right base
Dull percussion note at the left base
Fine inspiratory crackles at both bases
practice.e: A URTI has no focal chest findings. Bronchial breathing or focal crackles suggest pneumonia; dullness suggests an effusion or consolidation.

clues: runny nose, sore throat and dry cough

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Bronchial breathing is consolidation (pneumonia).
Dullness suggests effusion or consolidation.
Fine bibasal crackles suggest fibrosis or oedema.
A rub suggests pleurisy.

steps.x: **D. No focal abnormality.** URTI = clear chest.

practice.stem: A 29 year old woman has a 3 day history of sore throat, runny nose and cough. She is eating and drinking. Her temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 80 bpm, BP 116/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air. Her chest is clear.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
o: Viral PCR of a nasopharyngeal swab
practice.e: An uncomplicated URTI is a clinical diagnosis; tests do not change management. Bloods and CXR are only for severe cases.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: CXR is for severe cases.
Bloods are for severe cases.
Swabs do not change management.
PCR is not needed for an uncomplicated cold.

practice.stem: A 52 year old man has had a cold for 6 days. Over the last day he has developed a temperature of 39.0°C, breathlessness and right-sided chest pain on breathing in. His pulse rate is 108 bpm, BP 124/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 94% breathing air. Chest X-ray (see item resources).

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Clear lung fields; no consolidation, effusion or pneumothorax.

practice.q: Which is the most appropriate interpretation of the investigations?
practice.e: With emergency features, bloods and a CXR are done to exclude pneumonia. A clear film and only mildly raised markers fit a viral URTI; the pain is likely muscular from coughing.

steps.x: Emergency features prompted **bloods and a CXR**, which is clear.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: No consolidation on the film.
No blunting of the costophrenic angle.
Lung markings reach the edges.
No bat-wing shadowing or cardiomegaly.

steps.x: **E. Viral URTI without pneumonia.** Clear CXR excludes pneumonia.

practice.stem: A 33 year old man has a 2 day history of runny nose, blocked nose, sore throat and dry cough. He is otherwise well. His temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 80 bpm and BP 122/76 mmHg. His chest is clear. He asks for antibiotics as he has an important meeting.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Analgesia (paracetamol, ibuprofen) and review in 3-4 days if not improving
practice.e: An uncomplicated viral URTI is managed with self-care and a review in 3-4 days if not improving. Antibiotics are only for a suspected bacterial cause.

steps.x: Viral, well; patient pressure is not an indication.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: No bacterial features; amoxicillin will not help.
Clarithromycin is for a bacterial cause with penicillin allergy.
No bacterial cause is suspected.
Steroids have no role.

steps.x: **B. Paracetamol, ibuprofen and review in 3-4 days.** Self-care, not antibiotics.

practice.stem: A 28 year old woman has a 3 day history of a very blocked nose, clear rhinorrhoea and mild sore throat. She is taking paracetamol. Her temperature is 37.3°C, pulse rate 74 bpm and BP 114/68 mmHg. Her chest is clear. She wants something to clear her nose.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment for her nasal congestion?
practice.e: A nasal decongestant such as xylometazoline can help congestion in a URTI, for a short course only. Antibiotics and steroids do not help a viral cold.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Mupirocin is for staphylococcal carriage.
Antibiotics do not treat a viral cold.
Steroids have no role in a cold.
No bacterial cause suspected.

steps.x: **A. Xylometazoline nasal spray.** For no more than about 7 days.

practice.stem: A 36 year old man has an upper respiratory tract infection and his GP suspects a secondary bacterial throat infection. He had a widespread urticarial rash after penicillin as a child. His temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 92 bpm and BP 126/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic?
practice.e: For a suspected bacterial URTI, phenoxymethylpenicillin is first-line, but with penicillin allergy clarithromycin is the alternative.

clues: suspects a secondary bacterial throat infection

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Amoxicillin is a penicillin.
Cephalosporins risk cross-reactivity and are not the listed alternative.
Co-amoxiclav contains amoxicillin.
Penicillin V is first-line only if not allergic.

practice.stem: A 3 year old boy and his 35 year old father both catch parainfluenza virus. The father develops a hoarse voice and sore throat. The boy develops a barking cough and inspiratory stridor. The boy's temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 124 bpm and BP 94/58 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely explanation for the boy's stridor?
o: Children produce more mucus than adults
Parainfluenza targets the alveoli in children
Smaller airway radius magnifies the effect of mucosal swelling
The paediatric epiglottis is larger and floppier
practice.e: The paediatric subglottic airway is narrow, so the same laryngotracheal swelling causes a far greater rise in resistance, producing stridor.

steps.x: Mechanism: why the child and not the adult?
Same virus; the difference is **airway size**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Narrow paediatric airway** is disproportionately affected by swelling.

elim: Mucus volume does not cause stridor.
Croup affects the larynx and trachea, not alveoli.
Croup is viral; no bacterial superinfection here.
Epiglottic shape explains epiglottitis risk, not croup stridor.

steps.x: **D. Smaller airway radius.** Swelling in a narrow subglottis = stridor.

prompts.q: What is a URTI, which parts of the airway does it affect, and which viruses cause it?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: viral; name rhinovirus first.

points.p: Affects nose, sinuses, pharynx and larynx
points.why: Above the vocal cords and trachea.

points.p: Most commonly viral
Rhinovirus, coronavirus, adenovirus, influenza
Risk factors: winter, contact with infected people

prompts.q: Describe the symptoms and examination findings of a URTI.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the clear chest is the key negative.

points.p: Sore throat, rhinorrhoea, nasal congestion, sneezing, cough
points.why: Coryza is the cluster of nasal symptoms.

points.p: Low-grade fever
points.why: High fever suggests influenza or LRTI.

points.p: Erythematous throat
No focal chest findings

prompts.q: What is croup: cause, age, and the sound it makes?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: barking cough + stridor + 6 months to 6 years.

points.p: Caused by parainfluenza virus
Age 6 months to 6 years
Stridor: harsh inspiratory sound from laryngeal obstruction
Barking cough

prompts.q: What complications can follow a URTI, and which features suggest it has spread to the chest?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: ear and sinus are bacterial follow-ons; high fever, breathlessness, chest pain mean LRTI.

points.p: Sinusitis
Otitis media
Red flags: high fever, breathlessness, chest pain
Progression to LRTI or pneumonia

prompts.q: How do you tell a viral URTI from bacterial tonsillitis, sinusitis and pneumonia?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: exudate, duration and chest signs.

points.p: Bacterial tonsillitis: exudate, tender anterior nodes, no cough
points.why: A cough points away from strep.

points.p: Sinusitis: facial pain, purulent discharge, beyond 10 days
points.why: A cold settles within about a week.

points.p: Pneumonia: focal chest signs, high fever

prompts.q: How is a URTI diagnosed, and when do you investigate further?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: 'no investigation' unless the stem says severe.

points.p: Clinical diagnosis is the gold standard
Severe cases: blood tests and chest X-ray to exclude pneumonia

prompts.q: How is an uncomplicated URTI managed, and when is it reviewed?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: self-care beats antibiotics in nearly every URTI stem.

points.p: Self-care: paracetamol and ibuprofen
Review in 3-4 days if not improving
Nasal decongestant such as xylometazoline

prompts.q: If a bacterial cause is suspected, what is given, and what if the patient is penicillin allergic?

points.p: Phenoxymethylpenicillin (penicillin V)
Clarithromycin if penicillin allergic

prompts.q: Why does a URTI cause a runny, blocked nose, and why does it resolve on its own?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: inflammation, oedema, mucus; immune clearance in about a week.

points.p: Viruses infect nasal, pharyngeal and laryngeal mucosa
Local inflammation, oedema and increased mucus secretion
Self-limiting in about 1 week, driven by host immune response

prompts.q: Why does croup cause stridor, and why do secondary bacterial infections occur after a URTI?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: narrow subglottis; damaged mucosa and poor clearance.

points.p: Laryngotracheal inflammation and subglottic narrowing
Narrow paediatric airway disproportionately affected by swelling
points.why: Resistance rises steeply as radius falls.

points.p: Viral mucosal damage and impaired clearance let bacteria invade
points.why: Sinuses, or middle ear via Eustachian tube.

points.p: Eustachian tube route to the middle ear
points.why: Shorter and more horizontal in children.

glossary.URTI: Upper respiratory tract infection: infection of the nose, sinuses, pharynx or larynx.
glossary.LRTI: Lower respiratory tract infection: infection below the larynx, such as bronchitis or pneumonia.
glossary.Common cold: A mild viral URTI of the nose and throat, usually rhinovirus.
glossary.Coryza: Inflammation of the nasal lining causing a runny, blocked nose and sneezing.
glossary.Rhinovirus: The commonest cause of the common cold.
glossary.Adenovirus: A virus causing colds, sore throat and conjunctivitis.
glossary.Croup: Viral laryngotracheobronchitis in young children causing a barking cough and stridor.
glossary.Laryngotracheobronchitis: Inflammation of the larynx, trachea and bronchi: the formal name for croup.
glossary.Stridor: A harsh, high-pitched sound on breathing in, from narrowing of the upper airway.
glossary.Wheeze: A musical, mainly expiratory sound from narrowed small airways.
glossary.Subglottic: The part of the airway just below the vocal cords, the narrowest point in a small child.
glossary.Barking cough: A harsh, seal-like cough typical of croup.
glossary.Erythematous: Red, from increased blood flow due to inflammation.
glossary.Focal chest findings: Signs in one part of the lung, such as crackles or bronchial breathing, suggesting pneumonia.
glossary.Bronchial breathing: Harsh, hollow breath sounds over consolidated lung.
glossary.Consolidation: Lung air spaces filled with fluid or pus, appearing white on X-ray.
glossary.Otitis media: Infection of the middle ear behind the eardrum.
glossary.Tympanic membrane: The eardrum; red and bulging in acute otitis media.
glossary.Eustachian tube: The tube linking the middle ear to the back of the nose.
glossary.Sinusitis: Inflammation and infection of the paranasal sinuses.
glossary.Mucociliary clearance: The sweeping of mucus out of the airways by beating cilia.
glossary.Self-limiting: An illness that gets better on its own without treatment.
glossary.Xylometazoline: A decongestant nasal spray; use for no more than about a week to avoid rebound congestion.
glossary.Rhinitis medicamentosa: Rebound nasal congestion from overusing decongestant sprays.
glossary.Phenoxymethylpenicillin: Penicillin V: the first-line oral antibiotic if a bacterial cause is suspected.
glossary.Clarithromycin: A macrolide antibiotic used in penicillin allergy.
glossary.Dexamethasone: A long-acting corticosteroid given as a single oral dose to treat croup.
glossary.Epiglottitis: Bacterial infection of the epiglottis (classically Hib) with drooling, high fever and airway risk.
glossary.Bronchiolitis: RSV infection of the small airways in infants under 1, causing wheeze and crackles.
glossary.RSV: Respiratory syncytial virus, the main cause of bronchiolitis.
glossary.CRP: C-reactive protein, a blood marker that rises with inflammation and infection.
glossary.Safety-netting: Telling a patient which symptoms should make them seek help again, and when.
